baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Interprets enslaved culture and paternalism as contested forms within a system of domination.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Existing complete preface and initial paternalism paragraphs, plus Walter Johnson’s complete retrospective, within their recorded scopes. Paternalism is not a benign-slavery claim; Johnson’s consent/coercion criticism remains visible.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Makes the relation between slaveholding class power, economic organization and development a problem for Marxist historical interpretation.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Specific political-economy intervention mediated by N. Gordon Levin’s substantive review, selected opening pages. This is a contribution to a contested interpretation, not proof that every Marxist shared it, or a direct personal influence from Marx or Gramsci.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Johnson challenges Genovese’s paternalism/hegemony account and a sharp individual/collective resistance opposition (2001), then specifies objections about revolutionary aspiration, coercive force and resistance in “On Agency” (2003), without saying Genovese ignored enslaved agency.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Two separately dated primary interventions consolidated as one relationship. 2001 scholarly rereading: Johnson challenges Genovese’s paternalism/hegemony account and the sharp opposition between individual resistance and collective revolt, while affirming the book’s lasting value (2001). Complete scholarly rereading. Johnson argues for coerced rule and a continuum of resistance; he explicitly rejects the simplistic charge that Genovese denied enslaved people agency. Original historical examples and Roll, Jordan, Roll remain uncollated. Reading extent: Fresh complete review read through the final day-to-day resistance paragraph. Distinguishes Genovese’s hegemony argument from denying enslaved agency; criticizes paternalism, coerced rule and a strict individual/collective resistance opposition while affirming the book’s value. The original book and historical examples are not independently audited. 2003 “On Agency”: Johnson rejects three premises of Genovese’s resistance/hegemony account while rejecting the claim that Roll, Jordan, Roll simply ignores enslaved agency (2003). The named p. 117 criticism concerns revolutionary aspiration, culture versus coercive force, and the individual/collective distinction. It is not a denial that Genovese discussed resistance. Reading extent: Fresh primary pp113–114,117 and122–123 read; Genovese’s books were not newly read. These are not a single publication or a second independent edge. The original Genovese book and underlying historical examples are not independently collated.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Genovese adapts Gramscian hegemony to explain how paternalist relations could mediate slaveholding class rule, as Walter Johnson explicates (2001).
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Johnson’s own substantive account distinguishes Genovese’s use of hegemony from denying agency and then criticizes its application. Named-reader mediation is explicit; no certification of Genovese’s full book or Gramsci originals. The existing mixed Genovese/Gutman edge_162 stays.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Genovese’s analysis of slaveholding social relations and ideology supplies a resource in Davis’s account of slavery and abolition.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Davis1995 explicitly finds the Genovese/Fox-Genovese case convincing; their credit remains shared. Sinha2019pp152–153 separately identifies Genovese’s influence on the1975 Age of Revolution and their conversations as fellows. Named mediation for that earlier transmission, not fresh reading of either1970s book. Sinha’s speculative reverse Hegel transmission is not accepted. This resource coexists with Davis’s specific1995criticism.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Davis values Genovese’s recovery of Southern thought but questions his political alliance with conservatism and his treatment of the liberal tradition.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own1995review, concluding objection: Davis invokes liberal critics of human perfectibility and argues that dismantling public power can serve corporate interests. Praise of scholarship and shared concerns about market values remain explicit. These are Davis’s political/intellectual judgments about the three reviewed books, not an editorial judgment of Genovese’s whole career; books unread.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Faust identifies Genovese among the slavery scholars who redirected her early research and recalls his intellectual importance in the Southern Intellectual History Circle.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own2014 first-person account credits a plural cohort;own2023 retrospect recalls Genovese’s insights at meetings and explicitly assesses his account of ideology. Elizabeth Fox-Genovese retains intellectual and coauthor credit,especially for the later trilogy. This is a bounded scholarly resource,not sole mentoring or adherence to paternalism. Original books remain unread;2023 selected substantial indexed primary passages checked despite direct-page failures.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Faust rejects Genovese’s paternalism framework while arguing that its disappearance leaves unresolved questions about slaveholders’ self-justifying ideas.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own2023 address calls paternalism flawed and distances herself from rehabilitation of Genovese. She retains his acknowledgment of cruelty,his later revisions,and the problem of ideology that remains after rejection. Elizabeth Fox-Genovese is coauthor of the later master-class studies;criticism does not assign those books to Eugene alone or equate understanding enslavers with endorsement. Complete original books unread.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Identifies Roll, Jordan, Roll as the starting point for the contemporary debate on master-slave paternalism.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Explicit evaluative authorial note6 in displayed digital notes; a resource for a debate, not assent to all of Genovese’s conclusions. Coexists with Berlin’s particular2003 chronological-scope criticism.1974 title/year are as cited by Berlin; the2001 speech reading list uses a different1976 edition. Both original editions and full Berlin Prologue unread.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Questions the limited attention to slavery before1830 in Genovese’s nineteenth-century-centered historiography.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Only the fresh publisher opening extract of Berlin2003 article read. He groups Genovese with Kenneth Stampp, Stanley Elkins, John Blassingame, Robert Fogel and Stanley Engerman and acknowledges their sharp disagreements. Do not infer rejection of paternalism, statistics or Marxism from this temporal-scope criticism; complete article and underlying books unread.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Lears uses Genovese’s account of paternalism, accommodation and resistance to develop a historical analysis of hegemony.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own1985draws on Roll, Jordan, Roll1974pp585–665 and separately In Red and Black1970p369. He explicitly says his summary simplifies a complex argument; slaves’ dignity and resistance remain alongside accommodation. Whole books unread.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Lears questions the classification of slave protest as prepolitical and the risk of making planter hegemony too static.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own578parenthesis places Genovese’s formulation beside Gramsci’s teleological limits;586reports criticism of a monolithic planter image while crediting Genovese’s sensitivity. It coexists with substantive use, not rejection of Roll, Jordan, Roll as a whole.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: informs some historians’ analyses of consent and class relations
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Reception varies among Marxist historians. Genovese is an American example, not a British historian; do not attribute a shared Gramscian method to Thompson and Hobsbawm. Hobsbawm’s1974 review provides a specific British reception: he values Gramsci for studying rebellion while questioning parts of the intellectuals schema. It does not establish Thompson’s agreement or a uniform method.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Gramscian resources enter distinct Genovese and Gutman interpretations
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: One disputed application within a heterogeneous radical historiography, not the origin of the US New Left. Gutman pp. 584–585 explicitly quotes Gramsci through Tilly on elite perceptions of subordinate groups. Genovese’s hegemony application is supported here by Johnson’s retrospective account; a direct original Gramsci passage in Genovese remains unread. These are different mechanisms and evidence scopes.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: intersects and contends in interpretations of slavery, resistance, and power
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Black historians’ independent institutions and arguments are not treated as products of the New Left. Genovese’s preface acknowledges alternative national-culture readings; Johnson’s 2001 retrospective review contests consent/coercion in his account. This later assessment qualifies an earlier book without extending mapped coverage.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Fox-Genovese defends narrative interpretation and challenges Stone’s assumptions about crisis and progress
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Her December 1978 letter explicitly states that Tuchman does not subscribe to Marxism. This is a supportive critical intervention in reception, not an influence on the completed book or endorsement of every conclusion; Stone’s reply remains visible in the same source.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Genovese uses Fogel and Engerman’s statistical and analytical work
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: His acknowledgments explicitly credit their supplied work and Engerman’s manuscript reading. This resource does not imply acceptance of all their conclusions and does not cancel Gutman’s separate criticism of Time on the Cross.
relevant_group_routes.map_label: Fogel and Engerman’s research supplied to Genovese

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Slavery scholarship and source collections provide resources for Genovese
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: The preface and acknowledgments name Rawick, Levine and Litwack; permissions also identify Du Bois and Black historical source collections. This particular use respects Black history’s independent institutions and does not derive that field from the New Left.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Sinha reads Davis’s account of British antislavery’s social function as an application of Gramsci’s ideological-hegemony concept.
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Named Sinha2019p154 and note35(bookp379); she distinguishes Genovese’s slaveholder application, Davis’s British limit and Ashworth’s American extension while criticizing the explanatory consequences. Original Davis and Gramsci passages remain unread; no wholesale Marxist-school affiliation or agreement with Sinha inferred.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Lears identifies Gramsci’s account of cultural hegemony as a framework for rethinking power, consent and cultural meaning in American history.
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Own1985explicitly adopts a framework and vocabulary while declining an uncritical embrace of the revolutionary program. Hoare/Nowell Smith’s1971Prison Notebooks translation and Lawner’s1973Letters are specified witnesses, not the complete Italian corpus. Own2010recollection retains Genovese and Davis as interpreters in his graduate intellectual environment.
